question_text: A fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus is most likely to injure which nerve?
explanation_text: The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery wind around the surgical neck of the humerus.

question_text: A midshaft fracture of the humerus with wrist drop indicates injury to which nerve?
explanation_text: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove on the midshaft of the humerus; injury causes wrist drop.

question_text: Klumpke palsy typically results from injury to which spinal roots?
explanation_text: Klumpke palsy is a lower trunk (C8-T1) injury and may include Horner syndrome if T1 sympathetics are involved.

question_text: Which muscle is the only abductor of the vocal cords?
explanation_text: Posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor of the vocal folds and is therefore called the safety muscle of the larynx.

question_text: The middle meningeal artery enters the cranial cavity through which foramen?
explanation_text: The middle meningeal artery (maxillary artery branch) passes through foramen spinosum to supply the dura.

question_text: The thoracic duct typically drains into which venous site?
explanation_text: The thoracic duct drains lymph from most of the body into the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and subclavian veins).

question_text: A lesion of the right optic tract produces which visual field defect?
explanation_text: Each optic tract carries contralateral visual field information, so a right tract lesion causes left homonymous hemianopia.

question_text: Which cranial nerve nucleus lies in the midbrain and supplies a muscle that elevates the eyelid?
explanation_text: Levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by the oculomotor nerve; its nucleus is in the midbrain at the superior colliculus level.

question_text: Meckel diverticulum is a remnant of which embryonic structure?
explanation_text: Meckel diverticulum is a persistent vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct remnant, typically on the antimesenteric ileum.

question_text: Which of the following is a neural crest derivative?
explanation_text: Adrenal medulla chromaffin cells arise from neural crest; adrenal cortex is mesodermal.

question_text: The primitive streak appears in which germ disc layer and initiates gastrulation?
explanation_text: Gastrulation begins with primitive streak formation in the epiblast; epiblast cells ingress to form mesoderm and definitive endoderm.

question_text: Which wave of the jugular venous pulse corresponds to atrial contraction?
explanation_text: The a wave is produced by right atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve at end-diastole.

question_text: The first heart sound (S1) is produced primarily by closure of which valves?
explanation_text: S1 is due to closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves at the onset of ventricular systole.

question_text: Which of the following is the most important determinant of myocardial oxygen demand?
explanation_text: Myocardial O2 demand is driven mainly by heart rate, contractility, and wall tension (afterload/preload via Laplace).

question_text: Which lung volume cannot be measured by simple spirometry?
explanation_text: Residual volume remains in the lungs after maximal expiration and requires dilution or body-box methods, not spirometry alone.

question_text: The Bohr effect describes which of the following?
option_a: Increased PO2 decreases CO2 binding to hemoglobin
option_b: Increased PCO2 or H+ decreases hemoglobin affinity for oxygen
option_d: Fetal hemoglobin has lower oxygen affinity than adult hemoglobin
explanation_text: The Bohr effect: raised PCO2 and H+ shift the O2-Hb curve to the right, unloading oxygen in metabolically active tissues.

question_text: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is most useful because it:
option_b: Diverts blood from poorly ventilated alveoli
explanation_text: HPV matches ventilation and perfusion by constricting arterioles supplying hypoxic alveoli.

question_text: Clearance of which substance is the gold-standard measure of GFR?
explanation_text: Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR. PAH clearance estimates RPF.

question_text: ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct via which receptor and channel?
explanation_text: V2 receptor activation raises cAMP, inserting aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane of principal cells.

question_text: The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is closest to the equilibrium potential of which ion?
explanation_text: At rest, membrane permeability is highest to K+, so RMP lies near EK (about -90 mV), typically around -70 mV.

question_text: Saltatory conduction is a property of:
option_b: Myelinated axons at nodes of Ranvier
explanation_text: In myelinated fibers, action potentials jump between nodes of Ranvier, increasing conduction velocity.

question_text: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of glycolysis?
explanation_text: PFK-1 is the major regulatory (committed) step of glycolysis, inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.

question_text: Von Gierke disease (GSD I) is caused by deficiency of:
explanation_text: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency prevents hepatic glucose release, causing severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly.

question_text: NADPH generated by the pentose phosphate pathway is primarily used for:
explanation_text: The oxidative PPP produces NADPH for fatty-acid/cholesterol synthesis and to keep glutathione reduced, protecting RBCs from oxidative injury.

question_text: Phenylketonuria is most often due to deficiency of:
explanation_text: Classic PKU is PAH deficiency; phenylalanine and phenylketones accumulate, causing intellectual disability if untreated.

question_text: The urea cycle takes place primarily in which organ and which cellular compartments?
explanation_text: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and ornithine transcarbamylase are mitochondrial; later urea-cycle steps are cytosolic, mainly in hepatocytes.

question_text: Maple syrup urine disease is due to defective metabolism of which amino acids?
explanation_text: Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency causes accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine, with a burnt-sugar odor.

question_text: Which enzyme synthesizes the RNA primer during DNA replication?
explanation_text: Primase (DnaG in bacteria) lays down a short RNA primer so DNA polymerase can extend the chain.

question_text: Southern blotting detects which macromolecule?
explanation_text: Southern = DNA, Northern = RNA, Western = protein. Remember the mnemonic SNOW DROP.

question_text: Which vitamin deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy?
explanation_text: Thiamine deficiency in alcohol use disorder causes Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia).

question_text: Scurvy is due to impaired collagen cross-linking from deficiency of:
explanation_text: Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases required for stable collagen; deficiency causes bleeding gums and poor wound healing.

question_text: Which mediator is the most potent endogenous pyrogen among the following?
explanation_text: IL-1 and TNF act on the hypothalamus to raise the temperature set-point (fever). PGE2 is the proximal mediator in the hypothalamus.

question_text: Caseous necrosis is classically associated with which infection?
explanation_text: Caseous (cheese-like) necrosis is the hallmark of granulomatous TB (and some fungal) lesions.

question_text: Apoptosis is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:
explanation_text: Apoptosis is programmed death without inflammation; necrosis leaks contents and incites inflammation.

question_text: Which free-radical scavenger enzyme converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide?
explanation_text: SOD converts O2- to H2O2; catalase and glutathione peroxidase then convert H2O2 to water.

question_text: Metaplasia of respiratory epithelium in chronic smokers is typically:
explanation_text: Pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium is replaced by squamous epithelium (squamous metaplasia), a reversible adaptive change.

question_text: Reed-Sternberg cells are the hallmark of:
explanation_text: Binucleate CD15+/CD30+ Reed-Sternberg cells define classic Hodgkin lymphoma.

question_text: The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) producing BCR-ABL is classic for:
explanation_text: t(9;22) BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase defines CML and is the target of imatinib.

question_text: Auer rods are characteristically seen in:
explanation_text: Auer rods (fused azurophilic granules) are pathognomonic of myeloid blasts, especially AML.

question_text: Pernicious anemia is caused by autoimmunity against:
explanation_text: Loss of intrinsic factor from gastric parietal-cell destruction leads to B12 malabsorption and megaloblastic anemia.

question_text: Which translocations is associated with Burkitt lymphoma?
explanation_text: Burkitt lymphoma: MYC overexpression from t(8;14) (or variants t(2;8), t(8;22)). Starry-sky histology.

question_text: The most common site of hematogenous osteomyelitis in children is:
explanation_text: Sluggish metaphyseal loops make the metaphysis the preferred site in children; in adults vertebra is common.

question_text: Aschoff bodies are seen in which condition?
explanation_text: Aschoff bodies (foci of fibrinoid necrosis with Anitschkow cells) are pathognomonic of rheumatic carditis.

question_text: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules are a feature of:
explanation_text: Nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson) is characteristic of diabetic nephropathy.

question_text: Councilman bodies represent which process in the liver?
option_d: Councilman is a viral inclusion in neurons
explanation_text: Councilman (acidophil) bodies are apoptotic hepatocytes, classically in viral hepatitis.

question_text: Which gene is a classic tumor suppressor (two-hit hypothesis)?
explanation_text: RB is a tumor suppressor; both alleles must be inactivated (Knudson two-hit). RAS and MYC are proto-oncogenes.

question_text: AFP is an important tumor marker for:
explanation_text: AFP is raised in HCC and yolk-sac (endodermal sinus) tumor. PSA is prostate; calcitonin is MTC; CEA is colon (nonspecific).

question_text: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is caused by germline mutation of:
explanation_text: Germline TP53 mutation causes Li-Fraumeni: sarcomas, breast cancer, leukemia, adrenocortical carcinoma, brain tumors.

question_text: Psammoma bodies are classically seen in all EXCEPT:
explanation_text: Psammoma bodies: papillary thyroid ca, meningioma, papillary serous ovarian/endometrial ca, mesothelioma. Not follicular thyroid ca.

question_text: The most common malignant tumor of bone in children is:
explanation_text: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone sarcoma in adolescents, typically around the knee (metaphysis).

question_text: Granulomas with caseation and acid-fast bacilli are the tissue hallmark of:
explanation_text: TB produces caseating granulomas; sarcoid granulomas are typically non-caseating.

question_text: Which organism is acid-fast due to mycolic acids in the cell wall?
explanation_text: Mycolic acids make mycobacteria acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen / Auramine). They also confer resistance to many antibiotics.

question_text: The most common cause of community-acquired lobar pneumonia in adults is:
explanation_text: S. pneumoniae is the leading cause of typical community-acquired pneumonia (rusty sputum, lobar consolidation).

question_text: Which toxin of Clostridium tetani causes spastic paralysis?
explanation_text: Tetanospasmin blocks glycine and GABA release at inhibitory interneurons (Renshaw cells), causing unopposed motor activity.

question_text: Thayer-Martin medium is used to isolate:
explanation_text: Thayer-Martin is chocolate agar with antibiotics that suppress flora and allow pathogenic Neisseria to grow.

question_text: Which organism shows a positive string test and grows in alkaline peptone water?
explanation_text: V. cholerae is oxidase-positive, comma-shaped, grows in alkaline media, and shows a mucin string test.

question_text: Which hepatitis virus is a DNA virus?
explanation_text: HBV is a partially double-stranded DNA virus (Hepadnaviridae). HAV/HCV/HEV are RNA viruses.

question_text: Negri bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusions seen in:
explanation_text: Negri bodies in hippocampal neurons (and Purkinje cells) are diagnostic of rabies.

question_text: Which virus is associated with cervical carcinoma?
explanation_text: High-risk HPV 16 and 18 express E6/E7 that inactivate p53 and RB, driving cervical and other anogenital cancers.

question_text: The infective form of Plasmodium for humans is:
explanation_text: Mosquitoes inject sporozoites; these infect hepatocytes, then merozoites infect RBCs. Gametocytes infect the mosquito.

question_text: Hydatid cysts are caused by:
explanation_text: E. granulosus (dog tapeworm) causes cystic hydatid disease, most often in liver; rupture risks anaphylaxis.

question_text: Which immunoglobulin crosses the placenta and provides neonatal immunity?
explanation_text: IgG is the only antibody class that crosses the placenta (FcRn-mediated). IgM does not; secretory IgA is in breast milk.

question_text: Type I hypersensitivity is mediated by:
explanation_text: Type I (immediate) is IgE-sensitized mast cells/basophils releasing histamine. Anaphylaxis and atopy are examples.

question_text: DiGeorge syndrome is due to failed development of which pharyngeal pouches?
explanation_text: 3rd/4th pouch failure: no thymus (T-cell deficit) and no parathyroids (hypocalcemia), with conotruncal anomalies (22q11).

question_text: Which drug is a selective beta-1 agonist used for cardiogenic shock?
explanation_text: Dobutamine is a relatively selective beta-1 agonist used to increase cardiac contractility in cardiogenic shock/heart failure.

question_text: Atropine poisoning is treated with:
explanation_text: Physostigmine is a tertiary anticholinesterase that crosses the BBB and can reverse central and peripheral antimuscarinic effects.

question_text: Which of the following is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker?
explanation_text: Atracurium is a competitive nicotinic antagonist at the NMJ and undergoes Hofmann elimination; succinylcholine is depolarizing.

question_text: Which ACE inhibitor is a prodrug that requires hepatic activation?
explanation_text: Enalapril (and most -prils except captopril and lisinopril) is a prodrug converted to enalaprilat.

question_text: Digoxin toxicity is more likely in the presence of:
explanation_text: Hypokalemia increases Na/K-ATPase binding of digoxin and predisposes to arrhythmias. Treat with Digibind in severe toxicity.

question_text: Which antiarrhythmic is the drug of choice for acute PSVT (AV nodal reentry)?
explanation_text: Adenosine briefly blocks AV nodal conduction and is first-line for stable PSVT. Verapamil is an alternative.

question_text: Spironolactone can cause which endocrine side effect?
explanation_text: Spironolactone is an androgen-receptor antagonist and can cause gynecomastia; eplerenone is more selective.

question_text: Which antibiotic is associated with gray baby syndrome?
explanation_text: Neonates lack glucuronyl transferase; chloramphenicol accumulates and causes gray baby syndrome (shock, ashen color).

question_text: Vancomycin flushing (red man syndrome) is due to:
option_b: Direct histamine release from mast cells
explanation_text: Rapid infusion causes non-IgE histamine release. Slow the infusion and give antihistamines; it is not a true allergy.

question_text: Isoniazid neurotoxicity is prevented by supplementation with:
explanation_text: INH interferes with pyridoxine metabolism, causing peripheral neuropathy; prophylactic B6 is given, especially in at-risk patients.

question_text: Which benzodiazepine antagonist is used in benzodiazepine overdose?
explanation_text: Flumazenil is a competitive GABA-A benzodiazepine-site antagonist. Use cautiously (seizure risk in chronic users/TCA mix).

question_text: Lithium toxicity is more likely with which concurrent drug?
explanation_text: Thiazides cause compensatory proximal sodium/lithium reabsorption, raising lithium levels. NSAIDs and ACEIs also raise levels.

question_text: First-line drug for absence seizures is:
explanation_text: Ethosuximide (T-type Ca channel blocker) is first-line for uncomplicated absence. Valproate if combined with generalized tonic-clonic.

question_text: Rigor mortis typically first appears in which muscles?
option_b: Eyelids and small muscles of the face
explanation_text: Rigor appears first in small muscles (eyelids, face, jaw) and then progresses downward (Nysten's rule), resolving in the same order.

question_text: Postmortem caloricity may be seen in death due to:
explanation_text: Heat production can continue after death in infections, sunstroke, tetanus, and strychnine, so the body may feel warm (postmortem caloricity).

question_text: The most reliable early sign of death among the following is:
option_a: Cessation of respiration observed for 1 minute
explanation_text: Irreversible cessation of circulation (and respiration) is the traditional legal/medical criterion of somatic death.

question_text: Garlic-like odor of breath and luminous vomitus suggest poisoning with:
explanation_text: Yellow phosphorus causes garlic odor and luminescent vomitus; cyanide is bitter almond; OP is kerosene/garlic-like but not luminous.

question_text: The antidote of choice for acute organophosphate poisoning is:
explanation_text: Atropine blocks muscarinic effects; pralidoxime (2-PAM) regenerates AChE if given before aging of the enzyme-OP complex.

question_text: Cherry-red postmortem staining is classically seen in:
explanation_text: Carboxyhemoglobin gives cherry-red livor. H2S may cause similar discoloration; cyanide can also appear pink-red.

question_text: Informed consent in India is primarily governed in practice by which landmark principle/case theme?
option_a: Bolam test only without patient autonomy
option_b: Samira Kohli and emphasis on adequate information
explanation_text: Indian courts (e.g. Samira Kohli) require disclosure of risks/alternatives sufficient for a real choice; consent must be informed, not a formality.

question_text: Dying declaration is admissible under which Indian Evidence Act section?
explanation_text: Section 32 IEA makes dying declarations relevant. They need not be on oath or in presence of a magistrate, though magistrate recording is preferred.

question_text: Incidence is defined as:
option_a: All existing cases at a point in time
option_b: New cases in a defined period in a defined population
explanation_text: Incidence measures new events over time. Prevalence is a snapshot of existing disease (old + new).

question_text: A case-control study is best suited to calculate which measure of association?
option_c: Attributable risk in the population only
explanation_text: Case-control studies sample on disease status, so odds ratio is the appropriate association measure; RR needs incidence data.

question_text: Herd immunity is most effective for diseases that:
option_a: Have no carrier state and spread only human-to-human
explanation_text: Herd immunity protects susceptibles when a critical proportion is immune, provided transmission is person-to-person without a major animal reservoir.

question_text: Sensitivity of a screening test is:
explanation_text: Sensitivity = TP / (TP+FN). Specificity = TN / (TN+FP). PPV = TP / (TP+FP).

question_text: For a normally distributed variable, mean +/- 2 SD includes approximately what percentage of observations?
explanation_text: Empirical rule: 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD of the mean.

question_text: Which test is appropriate to compare means of two independent groups when data are normally distributed?
explanation_text: Unpaired (Student) t-test compares two independent means. Paired t-test is for before-after or matched pairs. Chi-square is for categorical data.

question_text: p-value is best interpreted as:
option_a: Probability that the null hypothesis is true
option_b: Probability of the observed (or more extreme) result if the null were true
option_c: Probability of making a type II error
explanation_text: A small p-value means the data are unlikely under H0. It is not the probability that H0 is true, nor a measure of effect size.

question_text: Under the National TB Elimination Programme, the currently preferred diagnostic test for pulmonary TB is:
explanation_text: India's NTEP uses molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostics (CBNAAT/TrueNat) rather than serology. Mantoux is not diagnostic of active TB.

question_text: The primary case definition used in pulse polio / AFP surveillance is:
option_a: Any case of flaccid paralysis in a child <15 years, or a suspected polio case at any age
explanation_text: AFP surveillance: sudden onset flaccid paralysis in under-15s (plus any suspected polio) is reported, with stool testing, to detect wild poliovirus.

question_text: BCG vaccine is which type of vaccine?
explanation_text: BCG is live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis (Danish/Pasteur strains). It is given intradermally at birth in the UIP.

question_text: Which vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy?
explanation_text: Live vaccines (MMR, varicella, yellow fever in some settings) are contraindicated in pregnancy. Inactivated vaccines and TT/Tdap are used as indicated.

question_text: Which cardiac biomarker is most specific for myocardial injury in current clinical practice?
explanation_text: Cardiac troponins are the most sensitive and specific markers of myocardial necrosis and are preferred over CK-MB for diagnosing MI.

question_text: The most common cause of acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction is:
option_b: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture with occlusive thrombus
explanation_text: STEMI is usually due to rupture or erosion of an atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed occlusive thrombosis.

question_text: Beck triad of cardiac tamponade consists of:
option_b: Hypotension, muffled heart sounds, raised JVP
option_c: Chest pain, pericardial rub, ST elevation
explanation_text: Beck triad: hypotension, muffled sounds, elevated JVP. Pulsus paradoxus and electrical alternans are additional clues.

question_text: First-line drug class for chronic HFrEF that has been shown to improve survival includes:
explanation_text: ACEI/ARB/ARNI, evidence-based beta-blockers, MRAs, and SGLT2 inhibitors improve survival in HFrEF. Digoxin may reduce hospitalizations but not mortality as primary therapy.

question_text: Infective endocarditis in IV drug users most often involves which valve?
explanation_text: Right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis is typical in injection-drug use; S. aureus is the leading organism.

question_text: Which finding is most characteristic of tension pneumothorax?
option_b: Tracheal deviation away from the affected side
explanation_text: Air under pressure collapses the lung and shifts the mediastinum and trachea to the contralateral side. This is a clinical emergency.

question_text: The strongest risk factor for COPD in India among the following is:
option_a: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in all cases
explanation_text: Cigarette (and biomass) smoke is the dominant risk factor for COPD. A1AT deficiency is important but uncommon.

question_text: Light criteria are used to distinguish:
explanation_text: Light criteria (pleural/serum protein and LDH ratios) classify pleural fluid as exudate or transudate.

question_text: The drug of choice for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is:
explanation_text: High-dose TMP-SMX is first-line for PCP. Adjunctive steroids are used if hypoxemia is significant.

question_text: Charcot triad of acute cholangitis includes:
option_a: Jaundice, fever, right upper quadrant pain
explanation_text: Charcot: RUQ pain, jaundice, fever. Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and mental status change (severe cholangitis).

question_text: The most sensitive and specific non-invasive marker of hepatocellular carcinoma among the following is:
explanation_text: AFP is the classic serum marker for HCC (also yolk-sac tumor). Imaging (multiphasic CT/MRI) is required for diagnosis in cirrhosis.

question_text: Celiac disease is associated with which HLA types?
explanation_text: Almost all patients with celiac disease carry HLA-DQ2 or DQ8. Absence of both makes celiac very unlikely.

question_text: The most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall is:
option_b: Ectopic ACTH from small-cell lung cancer
explanation_text: Iatrogenic (exogenous steroid) Cushing is the most common cause. Among endogenous causes, pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) leads.

question_text: In DKA, the anion-gap metabolic acidosis is primarily due to:
explanation_text: Ketone bodies (mainly beta-hydroxybutyrate) cause high-AG acidosis. Treatment is insulin, fluids, and potassium repletion.

question_text: Primary hyperparathyroidism classically presents with:
option_b: High calcium, low phosphate, high or inappropriately normal PTH
explanation_text: Parathyroid adenoma causes PTH-dependent hypercalcemia with phosphaturia (low phosphate). PTH-independent hypercalcemia suppresses PTH.

question_text: The most common cause of stroke overall is:
explanation_text: About 80-85% of strokes are ischemic. ICH and SAH are the major hemorrhagic types.

question_text: Guillain-Barre syndrome typically shows which CSF pattern?
explanation_text: CSF in GBS: elevated protein with normal (or near-normal) cell count, usually after the first week.

question_text: Which anti-epileptic is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia?
explanation_text: Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine) is first-line for classic trigeminal neuralgia.

question_text: The most common organism causing surgical site infection after clean-contaminated abdominal surgery is:
explanation_text: Gram-negative enteric flora (especially E. coli) predominate after clean-contaminated GI procedures. S. aureus leads in clean wounds.

question_text: Courvoisier law states that a painless palpable gallbladder with jaundice is unlikely to be due to:
option_b: Stone in the common bile duct
explanation_text: A distensible gallbladder implies a non-calculous distal obstruction (e.g. pancreatic head ca). Stones usually leave a fibrotic, non-distensible gallbladder.

question_text: The rule of nines is used to estimate:
explanation_text: Wallace rule of nines estimates % TBSA burned in adults (head 9%, each arm 9%, each leg 18%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18%, perineum 1%).

question_text: Parkland formula for burn fluid resuscitation in the first 24 hours is:
explanation_text: Parkland: 4 mL RL x kg x %TBSA; half in first 8 hours from time of burn, remaining half over next 16 hours. Titrate to urine output.

question_text: The most common site of peptic ulcer perforation is:
option_b: Anterior wall of first part of duodenum
explanation_text: Anterior duodenal ulcers perforate into the peritoneum; posterior ulcers may erode the gastroduodenal artery and bleed.

question_text: Virginity of the peritoneal cavity is lost in which of the following herniae that is always acquired?
option_d: Both indirect and femoral are congenital
explanation_text: Direct inguinal hernia is always acquired (Hesselbach triangle). Indirect may be congenital (patent processus vaginalis).

question_text: Boas sign (hyperesthesia below the right scapula) is associated with:
explanation_text: Boas sign is referred hyperesthesia in the right infrascapular region in acute cholecystitis.

question_text: The investigation of choice for suspected acute pancreatitis is:
option_b: Contrast-enhanced CT after 48-72 hours if severe/uncertain
explanation_text: Diagnosis is clinical plus lipase/amylase. CECT is used to assess necrosis/complications, typically after 48-72 h, not routinely at admission.

question_text: The most common type of renal calculus worldwide is:
explanation_text: Calcium oxalate stones are the most common. Struvite are infection (urease) stones; uric acid are radiolucent; cystine are rare (genetic).

question_text: Seminoma of the testis is most radiosensitive and typically presents in which age group?
explanation_text: Seminoma peaks in the 4th decade, is highly radiosensitive, and has a better prognosis than non-seminomatous GCT. AFP is not raised in pure seminoma.

question_text: The most common cause of bladder outlet obstruction in elderly men is:
explanation_text: BPH is the leading cause of LUTS and BOO in older men. Evaluate with IPSS, DRE, and PSA as indicated.

question_text: The most common site of hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage is:
explanation_text: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms in small perforators make the putamen the most common site of hypertensive ICH, followed by thalamus, pons, and cerebellum.

question_text: Extradural hematoma typically results from injury to which vessel?
explanation_text: EDH is often MMA laceration after temporal bone fracture, with lucid interval. Bridging-vein tears cause subdural hematoma.

question_text: Cushing triad of raised ICP includes:
explanation_text: Cushing reflex: raised BP, reflex bradycardia, and irregular breathing due to brainstem ischemia from high ICP.

question_text: The recommended daily elemental iron supplementation in pregnancy in India (Anemia Mukt Bharat / national guidance) is typically:
option_d: 200 mg for all women regardless of Hb
explanation_text: Standard prophylactic dose is 60 mg elemental iron with 500 mcg folic acid daily in pregnancy (higher therapeutic doses if anemic).

question_text: Physiological anemia of pregnancy is mainly due to:
option_b: Disproportionate rise in plasma volume over RBC mass
explanation_text: Plasma volume expands more than red-cell mass, lowering hematocrit. True iron deficiency is superimposed and common, but the dilutional effect is physiologic.

question_text: The most common cause of first-trimester miscarriage is:
option_d: Luteal phase defect in all cases
explanation_text: About half of early miscarriages show embryonic chromosomal anomalies (especially trisomy). Cervical incompetence causes mid-trimester losses.

question_text: HELLP syndrome is a severe form of preeclampsia characterized by:
option_a: Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets
explanation_text: HELLP: microangiopathic hemolysis, raised AST/ALT, thrombocytopenia. Delivery is the definitive therapy after stabilization.

question_text: The drug of choice for eclampsia seizure control is:
option_c: Phenytoin as first-line in all guidelines
explanation_text: MgSO4 (Pritchard or Zuspan regimen) is superior to diazepam/phenytoin for preventing recurrent eclamptic seizures.

question_text: The most common site of endometriosis is:
explanation_text: Ovaries are the most frequent site (chocolate cysts). Cul-de-sac, uterosacral ligaments, and pelvic peritoneum are also common.

question_text: Meigs syndrome consists of ovarian fibroma with:
option_a: Ascites and hydrothorax that resolve after tumor removal
explanation_text: Meigs: benign ovarian fibroma + ascites + right hydrothorax; fluid resolves after excision. Pseudo-Meigs can occur with other tumors.

question_text: The most common type of endometrial carcinoma is:
explanation_text: Type I endometrioid adenocarcinoma (estrogen-related) is the most common. Serous/clear cell are type II, more aggressive, p53-related.

question_text: The smallest diameter of the fetal skull is:
explanation_text: Suboccipitobregmatic (~9.5 cm) is the engaging diameter in well-flexed vertex presentation.

question_text: Active management of the third stage of labour includes:
option_b: Uterotonic at delivery of the anterior shoulder/baby plus controlled cord traction as per protocol
explanation_text: AMTSL: prophylactic uterotonic (oxytocin), delayed cord clamping as appropriate, and controlled cord traction when a trained attendant is present.

question_text: Bandl ring is a feature of:
explanation_text: A pathological retraction ring (Bandl) between the thinned lower segment and thickened upper segment indicates obstructed labour and impending rupture.

question_text: The most common cause of respiratory distress in a term neonate delivered by cesarean section is:
explanation_text: TTN (delayed clearance of lung fluid) is common after elective CS. RDS/HMD is mainly a preterm, surfactant-deficiency problem.

question_text: Vitamin K is given at birth to prevent:
explanation_text: Neonates have low vitamin K stores; IM vitamin K prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding (HDN).

question_text: Phototherapy for neonatal jaundice acts primarily by:
option_b: Converting bilirubin to water-soluble isomers excreted in bile/urine
option_d: Binding bilirubin in the gut as first action
explanation_text: Blue-green light produces lumirubin and other photoisomers that can be excreted without conjugation.

question_text: Koplik spots are pathognomonic of:
explanation_text: Koplik spots (white grains on erythematous buccal mucosa) appear 1-2 days before the measles rash.

question_text: A child with fever for 3 days, then rash starting after fever defervescence, is typical of:
explanation_text: Roseola: high fever for 3-5 days in an otherwise well infant, then defervescence and a rose-pink maculopapular rash.

question_text: The drug of choice for severe falciparum malaria in children (WHO/national severe malaria) is typically:
explanation_text: IV/IM artesunate is first-line for severe malaria, followed by a full oral ACT course. Primaquine is for hypnozoites (vivax/ovale), not severe falciparum treatment alone.

question_text: Birth weight typically doubles by which age?
explanation_text: Birth weight doubles by about 5 months and triples by 1 year. Height increases by 25 cm in the first year.

question_text: A child can sit without support at approximately:
explanation_text: Sits without support around 8 months; walks around 12-15 months. Always interpret in a developmental context.

question_text: The first permanent tooth to erupt is usually the:
explanation_text: Permanent first molars (6-year molars) erupt around 6-7 years, often before the central incisors.

question_text: APGAR score components include all EXCEPT:
explanation_text: APGAR: Appearance (color), Pulse, Grimace (reflex), Activity (tone), Respiration. Birth weight is not a component.

question_text: Bitot spots are a sign of deficiency of:
explanation_text: Bitot spots are foamy triangular conjunctival lesions of keratin debris, a classic sign of vitamin A deficiency (xerophthalmia).

question_text: The most common cause of blindness in India among the following is:
option_d: Diabetic retinopathy as the overall leader
explanation_text: Cataract remains the leading cause of preventable blindness in India. DR and glaucoma are important but not the overall majority.

question_text: Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction most often to:
explanation_text: Phlyctenules are type IV reactions, classically to staph or tuberculoprotein, seen as a nodule at the limbus.

question_text: The first-line topical drug class for primary open-angle glaucoma is commonly:
option_a: Pilocarpine as first choice in all patients
explanation_text: Prostaglandin analogues increase uveoscleral outflow and are typical first-line drops for POAG. Steroids can raise IOP.

question_text: Acute angle-closure glaucoma typically presents with:
option_b: Painful red eye, halos, mid-dilated oval pupil, high IOP
option_c: Painless sudden vision loss with RAPD from CRAO
explanation_text: Acute ACG is an emergency: severe pain, headache, nausea, colored halos, steamy cornea, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil.

question_text: Cherry-red spot at the macula is seen in:
option_b: Central retinal vein occlusion (classic blood and thunder only)
explanation_text: In CRAO the ischemic retina is pale while the thin fovea still shows choroidal red (cherry-red spot). Also seen in some storage disorders.

question_text: The earliest clinically detectable diabetic retinopathy lesion is usually:
explanation_text: Microaneurysms are the first ophthalmoscopic sign of NPDR. New vessels define proliferative disease.

question_text: Which vitamin is used in the AREDS formulation for intermediate AMD (along with antioxidants/zinc)?
option_b: Vitamins C and E (with zinc, copper, lutein/zeaxanthin in later formulas)
explanation_text: AREDS/AREDS2 antioxidant + zinc formulas reduce progression of intermediate AMD. Beta-carotene was replaced by lutein/zeaxanthin (smoker risk).

question_text: The most common organism in acute otitis media in children is:
explanation_text: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and M. catarrhalis are the leading AOM pathogens. Pseudomonas is typical of otitis externa / malignant OE.

question_text: Cholesteatoma is most dangerous because it:
option_b: Erodes bone and can cause intracranial complications
option_c: Only causes painless discharge without risk
option_d: Is a cholesterol granuloma of the pinna
explanation_text: Cholesteatoma is erosive squamous epithelium in the middle ear/mastoid; complications include facial palsy, labyrinthitis, and brain abscess.

question_text: Rinne test negative (BC > AC) with Weber lateralizing to the same ear suggests:
option_a: Sensorineural hearing loss on that side
option_b: Conductive hearing loss on that side
explanation_text: Negative Rinne = conductive loss. Weber goes to the worse conductive ear (or the better SNHL ear).

question_text: Little area (Kiesselbach plexus) is the most common site of:
explanation_text: Anterior bleeds from Kiesselbach plexus on the anterior septum account for most epistaxis. Posterior bleeds are more severe (sphenopalatine).

question_text: Samter triad consists of asthma, aspirin sensitivity, and:
explanation_text: AERD (Samter): aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease with nasal polyposis and asthma.

question_text: The most common cause of stridor in infants is:
option_c: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis as the overall leader
option_d: Acute epiglottitis in vaccinated cohorts as most common
explanation_text: Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital cause of inspiratory stridor; it usually improves with growth.

question_text: Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury typically causes:
option_a: Immediate airway obstruction requiring emergency tracheostomy in all cases
option_b: Hoarseness with the cord in the paramedian position
explanation_text: Unilateral RLN palsy: hoarse/breathy voice, cord in paramedian/cadaveric position. Bilateral abductor palsy threatens the airway.

question_text: A colles fracture is a:
option_a: Volar-displaced fracture of the distal radius (Smith)
option_b: Extra-articular distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation (dinner-fork)
explanation_text: Colles: FOOSH in elderly, extra-articular distal radius, dorsal tilt, radial shortening. Smith is volar displacement.

question_text: The most common complication of a scaphoid fracture is:
option_b: Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole
explanation_text: Blood supply to the scaphoid is distal-to-proximal; proximal pole fractures risk AVN and nonunion. Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox is a clue.

question_text: Fat embolism syndrome after long-bone fracture typically presents with:
option_a: Immediate hypotension only at the scene
option_b: Delayed (24-72 h) respiratory distress, petechiae, and neurological change
explanation_text: Classic triad after 1-3 days: hypoxemia, petechial rash (upper body), and cerebral involvement. Supportive care is mainstay.

question_text: The most common organism in acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in children is:
option_d: Kingella in all age groups as number one
explanation_text: S. aureus is the leading cause. Salmonella is classically associated with sickle cell disease. Pseudomonas with puncture wounds of the foot.

question_text: Potts spine most commonly affects which region of the vertebral column?
explanation_text: Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott) prefers the thoracolumbar junction; paravertebral abscess and gibbus are classic.

question_text: The most common type of scoliosis is:
option_c: Neuromuscular (cerebral palsy) as overall most common
explanation_text: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (especially right thoracic in girls) is the most common form.

question_text: Cauda equina syndrome is suggested by all EXCEPT:
option_d: Spastic paraparesis with extensor plantars as the typical finding
explanation_text: Cauda equina is a lower-motor-neuron lesion (areflexia, flaccid bladder). Extensor plantars and spasticity suggest cord (UMN) compression.

question_text: Garden classification is used for fractures of the:
explanation_text: Garden I-IV grades displaced vs undisplaced intracapsular neck-of-femur fractures and guides osteosynthesis vs arthroplasty.

question_text: Auspitz sign is classically positive in:
explanation_text: Pinpoint bleeding on removal of psoriatic scale (Auspitz) reflects dilated dermal papillae. Grattage and candle-grease signs are related.

question_text: Wickham striae are seen in:
explanation_text: Wickham striae are fine white lacy lines on LP papules (and oral LP). LP is the 6 Ps: planar, purple, polygonal, pruritic, papules, plaques.

question_text: Herald patch followed by a Christmas-tree distribution of oval plaques is typical of:
explanation_text: Pityriasis rosea: herald patch then truncal oval lesions along Langer lines. Often HHV-6/7 associated; self-limiting.

question_text: Honey-colored crusts on the face of a child suggest:
explanation_text: Non-bullous impetigo (S. aureus / S. pyogenes) produces golden crusts. Treat with topical or oral anti-staph/strep agents.

question_text: Tinea capitis in children is most appropriately treated with:
option_a: Topical clotrimazole alone as sufficient therapy
explanation_text: Hair-shaft infection needs systemic antifungals (griseofulvin or terbinafine depending on species). Topicals alone fail.

question_text: Nikolsky sign is typically positive in:
explanation_text: Pemphigus vulgaris (intraepidermal acantholysis, anti-desmoglein 3) shows Nikolsky sign. Bullous pemphigoid is subepidermal and Nikolsky-negative.

question_text: Dermatitis herpetiformis is strongly associated with:
explanation_text: DH is the cutaneous manifestation of gluten-sensitive enteropathy; IgA in dermal papillae. Dapsone plus gluten-free diet.

question_text: A major depressive episode requires symptoms for at least:
explanation_text: DSM-5 MDE: at least 2 weeks of depressed mood or anhedonia plus other symptoms causing impairment. Dysthymia/PDD is more chronic (2 years in adults).

question_text: First-line pharmacotherapy for bipolar I acute mania among the following is:
option_c: Benzodiazepine as sole long-term mood stabilizer
explanation_text: Mood stabilizers (lithium, valproate) and atypical antipsychotics treat mania. Antidepressant monotherapy can switch bipolar patients into mania.

question_text: Schneider first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia include:
option_a: Thought echo, thought insertion, running commentary hallucinations
explanation_text: First-rank: thought broadcast/insertion/withdrawal, third-person auditory hallucinations, delusional perception, made feelings/acts. Not pathognomonic but classic.

question_text: Clozapine is uniquely effective in treatment-resistant schizophrenia but requires monitoring of:
explanation_text: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis; mandatory ANC monitoring. Also watch for myocarditis, seizures, and metabolic syndrome.

question_text: The CAGE questionnaire is a screening tool for:
explanation_text: CAGE: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener. Two or more positive answers suggest problematic drinking.

question_text: Delirium tremens typically appears how long after stopping alcohol?
explanation_text: Seizures ~12-48 h; DT usually 48-72 h (up to 5 days) after last drink: fluctuating confusion, autonomic hyperactivity, hallucinations. Treat with benzos.

question_text: SSRI discontinuation syndrome is least likely with which agent (longest half-life)?
explanation_text: Fluoxetine and its metabolite norfluoxetine have very long half-lives, so withdrawal is uncommon. Paroxetine and venlafaxine are notorious for discontinuation symptoms.

question_text: MAC (minimum alveolar concentration) is a measure of:
option_b: Potency of an inhalational anesthetic (ED50 for immobility)
explanation_text: MAC is the alveolar concentration at 1 atm that prevents movement in 50% of subjects to a surgical stimulus. It is inversely related to lipid solubility/potency.

question_text: Malignant hyperthermia is most often triggered by:
option_d: Local anesthetics of the amide group
explanation_text: MH (RYR1) is triggered by suxamethonium and halogenated volatiles. Treat with dantrolene, stop trigger, hyperventilate with 100% O2.

question_text: The most cardiostable induction agent among the following is:
explanation_text: Etomidate preserves hemodynamics (useful in shock) but suppresses adrenal 11-beta-hydroxylase. Propofol causes vasodilation/hypotension.

question_text: The local anesthetic with the highest cardiotoxicity is:
explanation_text: Bupivacaine is highly lipid-soluble and binds cardiac sodium channels avidly; lipid emulsion is used for LAST. Levobupivacaine/ropivacaine are safer.

question_text: A spinal anesthetic typically acts on which anatomical space?
explanation_text: Spinal (intrathecal) injection is into CSF in the subarachnoid space, usually L3-L4. Epidural is outside the dura.

question_text: The gold-standard confirmation of endotracheal tube placement is:
option_d: Auscultation of the epigastrium being silent only
explanation_text: Sustained ETCO2 is the most reliable immediate confirmation. Clinical signs can mislead. CXR checks depth, not tracheal vs esophageal in the first seconds.

question_text: Mallampati class IV implies:
option_a: Soft palate, fauces, uvula, and pillars visible
option_b: Only hard palate visible (no soft palate/uvula)
explanation_text: Mallampati IV: only the hard palate is seen. Higher class predicts difficult laryngoscopy, but it is only one component of airway assessment.

question_text: Silhouette sign on a chest radiograph is used to:
option_b: Localize a lesion by loss of the outline of an adjacent soft-tissue structure
explanation_text: When two structures of similar density touch, their border is lost. E.g. right middle lobe consolidation silhouettes the right heart border.

question_text: The investigation of choice for suspected pulmonary embolism in a stable patient with normal renal function is:
option_c: V/Q scan as first-line in all patients
explanation_text: CTPA is the standard confirmatory test when PE is likely and contrast is safe. D-dimer is for ruling out PE in low/intermediate probability. V/Q if contrast contraindicated.

question_text: Deep sulcus sign on a supine chest radiograph suggests:
explanation_text: In the supine patient, air collects anteromedially and deepens the costophrenic sulcus (deep sulcus sign of pneumothorax).

question_text: Rigler (double-wall) sign on abdominal radiograph indicates:
explanation_text: Air on both sides of the bowel wall (Rigler) means free intraperitoneal air. Erect CXR is more sensitive for small pneumoperitoneum (air under diaphragm).

question_text: The investigation of choice for acute appendicitis in children / thin young patients when ultrasound is inconclusive is often:
option_b: Contrast CT or MRI depending on institution/pregnancy
explanation_text: US is first-line in children/pregnant women to avoid radiation. If needed, MRI (pregnancy) or low-dose CT is used. Plain films rarely diagnose appendicitis.

question_text: The imaging modality of choice for suspected acute ischemic stroke in the first hours (to exclude hemorrhage and select therapy) is:
option_b: Non-contrast CT head (with vascular imaging as per protocol)
option_d: Ultrasound of the fontanelle in adults
explanation_text: NCCT rapidly excludes ICH. CT angiography / perfusion or MRI DWI then guides thrombolysis/thrombectomy decisions.

question_text: An epidural hematoma on non-contrast CT typically appears as a:
option_b: Biconvex (lentiform) hyperdense extra-axial collection limited by sutures
explanation_text: EDH is lentiform and usually does not cross sutures (dura is adherent). SDH is crescentic and can cross sutures but not midline dural reflections.

question_text: Describe the formation of the brachial plexus. Add a note on Erb palsy.
marks:
The brachial plexus is formed by the ventral rami of spinal nerves C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1. These roots emerge between scalenus anterior and scalenus medius in the posterior triangle of the neck. Roots unite to form three trunks: upper (C5–C6), middle (C7) and lower (C8–T1). Each trunk divides into anterior and posterior divisions behind the clavicle. Divisions regroup around the axillary artery as three cords named by position: lateral, medial and posterior.

Branches to remember in an exam answer: dorsal scapular and long thoracic from roots; suprascapular and nerve to subclavius from the upper trunk; lateral pectoral and musculocutaneous plus the lateral root of median from the lateral cord; medial pectoral, medial cutaneous nerves of arm and forearm, ulnar and the medial root of median from the medial cord; upper and lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial from the posterior cord.

Erb palsy follows injury at Erb's point (C5–C6), typically birth traction or a fall on the shoulder. The arm hangs adducted and internally rotated with the elbow extended, forearm pronated and wrist flexed — waiter's tip. Loss reflects suprascapular, axillary and musculocutaneous paralysis. Klumpke palsy (C8–T1) is a useful contrast: intrinsic hand wasting and a possible Horner syndrome if T1 white rami are involved. Close with prefixed (C4) or postfixed (T2) variants if marks remain.
